docs.title: Course work for 113475 Software Defined Infrastructure
docs.text: This documentation is meant to supplement the submitted code for the Software defined Infrastructure lecture exercises.

docs.title: Exercise solutions
docs.text:
All solutions are documented and can be navigated to via the sidebar to the left. There is a page for each exercise, containing entries which detail the exercise description, document the implemented solution, and a verification of the intended results.

Before viewing the solutions, it is advisable to read through the 0. Preliminaries section. It details some information about used commands, the environment the solutions were implemented in, etc.

The documentation has been written as documentation of results, but in a manner that can be followed along to reproduce said results. If exercises build on each other, previous solution approaches are presumed to be known and won't be rehashed in detail for each individual documentation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To follow the solutions provided, please ensure the following prerequisites are met:

  • Generating SSH Key-Pair
  • Install Terraform
  • Hetzner Signup
  • Generating an API Token

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: To facilitate more efficient interaction with the CLI tools used when creating cloud infrastructure, some aliases have been created. These are documented here in case they show up in screenshots of the conducted steps:

docs.title: SSHDM
docs.text:
alias sshdm="ssh -A -i ~/.ssh/hdm"

The public / private key-pair hdm was used during the exercise period. Since multiple key-pairs were available on the host system, an alias was created to make connecting to the Hetzner instances easier. The flag -i passes the specified private key file which will be used to authenticate against the server, while -A enables ssh-agent forwarding.

docs.title: VCI
docs.text:
alias vci='check-jsonschema --schemafile https://raw.githubusercontent.com/canonical/cloud-init/main/cloudinit/config/schemas/schema-cloud-config-v1.json'

Short for validate cloud-init, this alias was used to shorten the call to a third-party validation utility. Since the cloud-init package is not available for the system used during course work, the official JSON schema by Canonical was used to validate yaml configurations via check-jsonschema.

docs.title: Init script (init.sh)
docs.text:
The script inits.sh was written to facilitate easy module creation. It creates an exercise directory, copies the top level .env file and template Terraform code, and runs terraform init in the newly created directory: 

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── init.sh
    └── ...

docs.title: Apply script (apply.sh)
docs.text:
A script to prepare the shell and call terraform apply is provided in the Terraform directory:

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── apply.sh
    └── ...

It can be called with any exercise number as a command line argument. The script will source the .env file in the directory of the provided exercise number and call both terraform init and terraform apply from inside the directory.

The script was written to make the exercise results easily reproducible from the course work home directory (Terraform).

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
Templates can be found in the Modules directory:

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── Modules
    └── ...

Different modules have been created based on the provided templates, which are used throughout the project. To learn more, visit: - Terraform - Modules

docs.title: .env.template
docs.text:
This template contains the environment variables which are used throughout all solutions. Copy the template into the desired exercise directory and change the contents to contain your secrets. Rename the file to .env and source it to reproduce the documented results.

To learn more, visit: - Dotenv - The Linux Documentation Project - Sourcing a file

docs.title: Conf
docs.text:
The file Modules/Config/config.tf contains commonly used values, including SSH-keys of authorized users for the servers created when running the exercise solutions. If you wish to add an SSH-key, it is sufficient to add it to the authorizedKeys output directive, it will be applied to all exercise solutions:

output "authorizedKeys" {
  type = map(string)
  value = {
    neubert = "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAII12SWradHBuyiHJDTJmulP9LMsEeyXajvaCnZxgtKh0 sn067@hdm-stuttgart.de"
    goik    = "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIKY24AeEibQGSMPtstaN4REByLCM3kzjM//apEZ9WyUB goik@hdm-stuttgart.de"
  }
}

The file has been committed to version control for easy reproducibility and to allow a complete recreation of the local setup for grading purposes.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The file Modules/Firewall/firewall.tf contains common firewall rules, which can be added to the dynamic rule creation present in Templates/main.tf.template:

resource "hcloud_firewall" "TEMPLATE" {
  name = "TEMPLATE"

  dynamic "rule" {
    for_each = {
      for name in [TEMPLATE_ADD_RULE_NAMES_HERE] : name => module.firewall.firewall_rules[name]
    }
    content {
      description = rule.value.description
      direction   = rule.value.direction
      protocol    = rule.value.protocol
      port        = rule.value.port
      source_ips  = rule.value.source_ips
    }
  }
}

One example of a common firewall rule (SSH-Traffic via 22):

locals {
  firewall_rules = {
    ssh = {
      description = "Allow SSH"
      direction   = "in"
      protocol    = "tcp"
      port        = "2222"
      source_ips  = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]
    }
    ...

These rules are accessible via the modules output directive:

output "firewall_rules" {
  description = "Reusable firewall rule definitions"
  value       = local.firewall_rules
}

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The file Modules/Server/server.tf contains common server attributes, which can be added to the server resource present in Templates/main.tf.template:

resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = module.server.serverName_g01
  image        = module.server.serverImage
  server_type  = module.server.serverType
  location     = module.server.serverLocation
  ssh_keys     = [for key in hcloud_ssh_key.sshKeys : key.id]
}

These default values are accessible via the modules output directive, of which this is one example:

output "serverType" {
  description = "The cheapest server Type (cx23)"
  value = "cx23"
}

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 19 Cloud-init for starters

docs.title: Cloud-init for starters
docs.text: Follow Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction and assemble a corresponding cloud-init script. Use the package_reboot_if_required: true directive in favor of an explicit reboot command. Use the Hetzner WEB Gui for manual server creation. Copy-paste your cloud-init script into the respective text field.

docs.title: Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config
docs.text: Summary of Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction.

docs.title: Step 1 - Insert first line
docs.text:
The cloud-init config uses YAML ("YAML Ain't Markup Language") as markup language. The file must start with a comment on the first line so that the code is interpreted as cloud-config by the server:

#cloud config

docs.title: Step 2 - Create user
docs.text: After the initial comment, let us start by creating a new admin user with sudo privileges and pre-configured SSH key.

docs.title: Step 3 - Update packages
docs.text: The first thing we do is an update of the package lists and installed packages. A fresh copy of Linux may have outdated packages with critical security vulnerabilities. In this step, you could install necessary packages for your projects too.

docs.title: Step 4 – Harden SSH
docs.text: We need to create a new file in sshd_config.d. Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config are automatically overwritten by any *.conf file within the sshd_config.d directory. - Deactivate the root login - Enable user for SSH - Change the default port for SSH - Deactivate password authentication - Automatic disconnection in case of incorrect login - Deactivate unused functions

docs.title: Step 5.1 - Configure fail2ban
docs.text: To secure the SSH network protocol, use fail2ban against brute force attacks

docs.title: Step 5.2 – Enable ufw
docs.text: Make sure you allow the respective SSH port.

docs.title: Step 6 – Create the server
docs.text: Open the Hetzner Console, select your project and create a server. In the "Cloud config" text box, enter the configuration you just created.

docs.title: Cloud-init configuration
docs.text:
To create the configuration, follow the instructions laid out in Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config. The page provides the full configuration necessary to create the basic server instance via cloud-init.

Cloud-init generates its own config file 50-cloud-init.conf automatically, which enables password login by default:

To ensure the desired SSH configuration takes effect, an additional parameter has to be added to prevent password login from being enabled:

ssh_pwauth: false

docs.title: Verifying the configuration
docs.text: To verify the configuration was created correctly, run the schema validation:

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
To create the server, log into the Hetzner Console, select a project, and navigate to the Servers tab in the sidebar.

There a server can be bought and created manually. Paste the cloud-init configuration in the Cloud config text box and buy the server.

Note: No SSH keys were provided manually, since the configuration will add them to authorized_keys automatically.

docs.title: Logging into the server
docs.text:
After waiting for the script to run, log into the newly created server. Since we changed the port SSH runs on, we have to specify -p 2222:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/hdm -p 2222 holu@167.233.84.111

Note that a login as user root is no longer possible:

Logging in has to be done as the user holu:

Attempting a login without a permitted public key fails without allowing password login:

Logging in was successful, confirming the cloud-init configuration was loaded. The specified SSH keys were placed into the server's authorized_keys file:

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The configuration was supposed to set up a simple firewall, allowing only incoming SSH traffic to establish a connection.

The firewall created via cloud-init drops all packets except SSH traffic. ICMP is usually enabled by default if a server is created via the Hetzner GUI, but pinging the server for example doesn't work anymore since the firewall rules don't allow them through:

docs.title: Fail2Ban
docs.text:
In addition, fail2ban was set up. Repeated failed attempts are already penalized by the system, meaning fail2ban doesn't register the unsuccessful tries:

It is possible to confirm the tool was still set up by checking the file jail.local:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 20 Cloud-init by Terraform

docs.title: Cloud-init by Terraform
docs.text: Re-use your Cloud-init script from Cloud-init for starters. This time follow Figure 1106, “Terraform triggering Cloud-init” using Terraform for executing Cloud-init rather than Hetzner's WEB GUI.

docs.title: Server creation with Terraform
docs.text:
To avoid having to create the server manually, server creation via Terraform was set up.

Run the following command in the directory 20. Cloud-init by Terraform or execute the apply.sh script with the command line argument 20 to create the server via Terraform.

terraform init && terraform apply

docs.title: Cloud provider
docs.text:
To be able to access the Hetzner API, the hcloud cloud provider needs to be initialized:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = {
      source = "hetznercloud/hcloud"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 0.13"
}

hcloud: The provider hetznercloud/hcloud allows interfacing with Hetzner's infrastructure via Terraform. To learn more, visit: - Terraform Registry - Hetzner Cloud Provider

docs.title: Hetzner Cloud API token
docs.text:
To be able to purchase a server instance, the generated API token (as per Prerequisites) has to be read from the shell environment:

provider "hcloud" {
token = var.hcloud_token
}

To be able to source the token from a confidential .env file, follow the instructions in the Templates preliminary. Alternatively, you can export the secret directly to be stored as an environment variable in your current shell session:

export TF_VAR_hcloud_token=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE

To learn more, visit: The Linux Documentation Project - Bash Variables

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
# Create the server
resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = "g01"
  image        = var.serverImage
  server_type  = var.serverType
  location     = "nbg1"

  # Post server creation init script
  user_data    = file("cloud-init.yaml")
}

To read more about server resource creation, visit:

  • Terraform - Resources
  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_server

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Commonly used values have been stored in variables for ease of access:

variable "hcloud_token" {
  description = "Hetzner API token"
  type = string
  nullable = false
  sensitive = true
}

variable "serverImage" {
  description = "Server image"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "debian-13"
}

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

To learn more about Terraform variables, visit: Terraform - Variables

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
To be able to connect to the server immediately after the init-script has finished, an output directive was added in the file output.tf. It outputs the IPv4 address the server was assigned:

output "ip" {
  value = hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address
}

To learn more about Terraform output, visit: Terraform - Output

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The resulting server configuration was the same as described in Exercise 19. Results, except for the following:

  • A cheaper server type was selectable via the API, meaning the server ran on a machine with fewer resources.

Terraform allows creation of the server type Cost-Optimized CX23:

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

Servers of type CX23 are only available in limited amounts and sometimes not selectable via the GUI:

  • The deployment was now possible via Terraform, meaning the need for manual GUI interaction was gone.

This means the deployment can be done via shell and therefore automated:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 21 - Enhancing index.html generation

docs.title: Enhancing index.html generation
docs.text:
We extend our exercise Cloud-init by Terraform: - We recently cheated by creating an invalid HTML file:

echo "I'm Nginx @ $(curl -4 https://ifconfig.me) created $(date -u)" > /var/www/html/index.html

This time start from a proper tpl/index.html template file:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Template demo</title>
  </head>
  <body>                                     <!-- To become e.g. Sunday 08 Nov 2026 at 18:08 --->
    <h1>Terraform template file demo created ${creationDate}.</h1> 
    <p>This is server <b>${serverName}</b> having IP addresses:</p>
     <ul>
       <li>IPV4: <a href="http://${ipv4Address}">${ipv4Address}</a></li>          <!-- To become e.g. 2a01:4f8:c016:9b2::/64 -->
       <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[${ipv6Address}]">${ipv6Address}</a> from subnet ${ipv6Subnet}</li>
     </ul>
  </body>
</html>
  • Use Terraform's templatefile(...) function to replace all five variables by their respective values using Terraform for generating a gen/index.html file.
  • Use Cloud-init to transfer the generated index.html file to its respective location on your destination server. Nginx should then be happily picking it up.

docs.title: Setup (setup.tf)
docs.text: The project was created via the init.sh script, which created the base directory and the setup.tf file: Assume this script was run to create the following exercises. If anything was altered or omitted, the setup section of that exercise's solution page will specify which steps were taken.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
This file contains the base components used across many exercises, such as the required providers:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = ...
    local = {
      source = "hashicorp/local"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
}

In addition to the hcloud provider (see Ex. 19. Cloud-init for starters/1. Solution), the provider for local file interfacing is necessary:

local: The local provider by Hashicorp enables use of functions that operate on the local file system. To lean more, visit: - Terraform Registry - Hashicorp Local Provider

docs.title: Api Token
docs.text: The API token was created in the same manner as it was in Ex. 19. Cloud-init for starters/1. Solution.

docs.title: SSH Keys
docs.text:
The SSH keys allowed to access the server were imported via setup.tf.template:

# Load the common configuration
module "config" {
  source = "../Modules/Conf"
}

# Set up SSH keys
resource "hcloud_ssh_key" "sshKeys" {
  for_each   = module.config.authorizedKeys
  name       = each.key
  public_key = each.value
}

To learn more, visit: - Terraform Registry - hcloud_ssh_keys Resource

docs.title: index.html
docs.text:
The index.html template from the exercise description was copied into the directory 21. Enhancing index.html generation/templates. It contains the following interpolation sequences for which values will be provided later:

- ${creationDate}
- ${serverName}
- ${ipv4Address}
- ${ipv6Address}
- ${ipv6Subnet}

These sequences will be replaced by the templatefile function.

To learn more, visit: - Hashicorp - templatefile function

docs.title: cloud-init.yaml
docs.text:
The cloud-init.yaml template was created in the directory 21. Enhancing index.html generation/templates. The configuration was written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) beforehand and then wrapped in a call to ${yamlencode(). This was done to prevent indentation problems which can occur during string interpolation. To learn more, visit: - HashiCorp - yamlencode - HashiCorp - Terraform language types and values

To enable our webserver to access the dynamically generated index.html file, we need to copy it into the /var/www/html directory. We also set permission so the file can be read by the reverse proxy we will use to serve the content (nginx).

write_files = [
  {
    content     = "${html}"
    path        = "/var/www/html/index.html"
    permissions = "0644"
    owner       = "root:root"
  }
]

To learn more, visit: - Cloud-init - Write files - Linux Foundation - File permissions

All that was left to do is write the instructions for the webserver to be installed and run:

packages = ["nginx"]
runcmd = [
    "systemctl enable nginx",
    "systemctl start nginx"
  ]

docs.title: Network configuration
docs.text:
The webpage is supposed to display the webserver's IP addresses, which requires us to create a resource for each IP type:

resource "hcloud_primary_ip" "ipv4" {
  name        = "primary-ipv4"
  location    = module.server.serverLocation
  type        = "ipv4"
  auto_delete = true
}

resource "hcloud_primary_ip" "ipv6" {
  name        = "primary-ipv6"
  location    = module.server.serverLocation
  type        = "ipv6"
  auto_delete = true
}

It is important to provide both resources with the same location, since the IPs need to be located in the same datacenter for the server creation to work. We set auto_delete to true. The IP addresses will be deleted by Hetzner once the servers no longer exist (i.e. you call terraform destroy).

To learn more, visit: - Terraform registry - hcloud_primary_ip

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
To allow web traffic, we need to allow inbound HTTP traffic. Additionally, set up SSH access and whitelist ICMP packets for easier server access and simpler monitoring. Add the names "ssh", "icmp", "http" to the list of common firewall rules inside the firewall resource created by the init.sh script:

for name in ["ssh", "icmp", "http"] : name => module.firewall.firewall_rules[name]

docs.title: index.html
docs.text:
To create the static webpage nginx should serve under the server's IP the file needs to generated by interpolating the strings listed in Templates - index.html This can be achieved via the previously mentioned templatefile function. It can replace content in a local file and save the generated output.

The function takes as many arguments as should be replaced as a key-value pair. It matches the provided keys against strings to be interpolated and replaces them with the associated value. We need to pass the attributes of the previously created IP resources to this function to replace the placeholders in the template. This needs to happen after resource creation of the IPs, since the ouput will be a static html file which requires the values to be hard-coded in.

resource "local_file" "index" {
  content = templatefile("templates/index.html", {
    creationDate = timestamp()
    serverName   = module.server.serverName_g01
    ipv4Address  = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv4.ip_address
    ipv6Address  = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.ip_address
    ipv6Subnet   = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.ip_network
  })
  filename = "gen/index.html"
}

The generated output will be saved to gen/index.htlm:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <title>Template demo</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Terraform template file demo created 2026-11-10T12:10:43Z.</h1>
<p>This is server <b>g01</b> with IP addresses:</p>
<ul>
    <li>IPV4: <a href="http://2.31.146.28">2.31.146.28</a></li>
    <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::]">2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::</a> from subnet 2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::/64</li>
</ul>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: cloud-init.yaml
docs.text:
The generated html file can now be passed into our cloud-init config. We need to provide the parameter html with the previously generated file accessible via local_file to interpolate "${html}".

resource "local_file" "cloud-init" {
  content = templatefile("templates/cloud-init.yaml", {
    html = local_file.index.content
  })
  filename = "gen/cloud-init.yaml"
}

The generated output will be saved to gen/cloud-init.yaml:

#cloud-config

"packages":
- "nginx"
"runcmd":
- "systemctl enable nginx"
- "systemctl start nginx"
"write_files":
- "content": |-
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
    <head>
        <title>Template demo</title>
    </head>
    <body>
    <h1>Terraform template file demo created 2026-11-10T12:10:43Z.</h1>
    <p>This is server <b>g01</b> with IP addresses:</p>
    <ul>
        <li>IPV4: <a href="http://2.31.146.28">2.31.146.28</a></li>
        <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::]">2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::</a> from subnet 2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::/64</li>
    </ul>
    </body>
    </html>
  "owner": "root:root"
  "path": "/var/www/html/index.html"
  "permissions": "0644"

docs.title: Verifying the output
docs.text:
To verify the generated cloud-init.yaml file, we can target the local file creation explicitly without creating the server resource. Supply the option -target=local_file.cloud-init when running terraform apply. This will only execute the resource creation of the cloud-init file, as well as all other operations it depends on:

This confirms the file is correctly encoded.

Note:

This already creates the IPs on Hetzner's end, since the cloud-init creation depends on the index.html creation, which in turn depends on the IP address resources. Run terraform destroy after this step!

docs.title: Server Creation
docs.text:
To use the common server parameters, load the server module:

module "server" {
  source = "../Modules/Server"
}

We then instantiate the server resource with the common parameters and resources, as well as the IP addresses and cloud-init configuration we created in the previous steps.

resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = module.server.serverName_g01
  image        = module.server.serverImage
  server_type  = module.server.serverType
  location     = module.server.serverLocation
  ssh_keys     = [for key in hcloud_ssh_key.sshKeys : key.id]
  firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.nginx.id]

  public_net {
    ipv4 = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv4.id
    ipv6 = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.id
  }

  user_data = local_file.cloud-init.content
}

To learn more, visit: - Terraform Registry - hcloud_server Primary IPs

Note:

The combination of the default server type cx23 and the default location nbg1 might not be available. If this occurs, you can try another location (e.g. fsn1). Keep in mind, the location declared in the IP resources must be changed accordingly!

docs.text: Logging in as root via SSH was possible as intended:

docs.text: Pinging the server was possible as well:

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text: Accessing the webserver was possible via HTTP, meaning a TCP connection on port 80 was able to be established as intended. See Result - Web Server

docs.title: IP addresses
docs.text:
The server was assigned two IP addresses:

These can be used to confirm the validity of our generated index.html landing page in the following section.

docs.title: nginx
docs.text: The nginx package was installed and the service was run by the cloud-init configuration:

docs.title: Static webpage (index.html)
docs.text: The webpage was accessible via HTTP through the browser. It contained the correct data, which means the interpolated file was served as intended:
